cloze.text: The {{c1::maxillary central incisor}} is the largest of all incisors, with a broad, {{c2::shovel}}-shaped crown and a prominent {{c3::cingulum}}.
On the maxillary central incisor, the {{c1::mesioincisal}} angle is sharp and the {{c2::distoincisal}} angle is rounded.
The maxillary central incisor is a common site for {{c1::trauma}} in kids and is prone to {{c2::attrition}} in deep overbites.
The {{c1::maxillary lateral incisor}} has a deep lingual fossa and pit and a narrow crown; peg laterals are possible.
The maxillary lateral incisor is the {{c1::second}} most commonly congenitally missing tooth (after {{c2::3rd molars}}).
Clinical tip, maxillary lateral incisor: check for caries in the {{c1::lingual pit}}; a {{c2::peg lateral}} may require cosmetic restoration.
The {{c1::maxillary canine}} has the longest root in the mouth and one sharp cusp.
The two lingual fossae of the maxillary canine are separated by a {{c1::lingual ridge}}.
The maxillary canine is the {{c1::second}} most commonly impacted tooth.
The maxillary canine is critical for esthetics and occlusion ({{c1::canine guidance}}); it may erupt ectopically ({{c2::palatal or buccal}}).
The maxillary 1st premolar's two roots are {{c1::buccal and palatal}}; it has 2 well-defined cusps.
The maxillary 1st premolar has a distinct {{c1::mesial}} root concavity and {{c1::mesial}} marginal groove.
Clinical tip: use care when scaling the {{c1::mesial}} surface of the maxillary 1st premolar (root concavity, often missed).
The maxillary 2nd premolar has {{c1::1}} root and 2 cusps (buccal and palatal) that are more {{c2::equal in size}}, a shorter central groove, and a more rounded crown.
The maxillary 2nd premolar is easier for scaling and instrumentation and less prone to {{c1::furcations}} (single root).
The maxillary 1st molar's three roots are {{c1::2 buccal and 1 palatal}}.
A possible 5th cusp of the maxillary 1st molar is the {{c1::Cusp of Carabelli}}, on the {{c2::mesiolingual}} cusp.
The {{c1::maxillary 1st molar}} has the largest crown in the dentition and is the most important tooth for occlusion.
On the maxillary 1st molar, the {{c1::palatal}} root is longest; the {{c2::palatal and mesial}} furcations are hardest to access.
The maxillary 2nd molar has 3 roots, 3–4 cusps, and a crown that is {{c1::rhomboid or heart}}-shaped.
The heart-shaped form of the maxillary 2nd molar is missing the {{c1::distolingual (DL)}} cusp.
The maxillary 2nd molar often resembles the 1st molar but smaller; watch for the {{c1::mesial}} furcation during perio exams.
The maxillary 3rd molar often has {{c1::fused}} roots, a smaller crown, and more grooves and supplemental anatomy.
The maxillary 3rd molar is often {{c1::impacted or missing}}; if erupted, it may be hard to clean and prone to decay.
The {{c1::mandibular central incisor}} is the smallest and most symmetrical tooth, with a straight incisal edge, single root, and shallow lingual surface.
The mandibular central incisor is the most difficult tooth to distinguish {{c1::left from right}} and a common site for {{c2::lingual calculus}} buildup.
The mandibular lateral incisor is slightly larger than the central; its incisal edge curves {{c1::distally}} (twisted appearance) and it has a subtle root concavity.
Clinical tip: use the {{c1::distal tilt}} to identify the mandibular lateral incisor; it is slightly harder to instrument due to its angle.
The mandibular canine has a long crown and {{c1::1}} root, which may be {{c2::bifurcated}}; it has smoother lingual anatomy than the max canine.
The mandibular canine is less prominent in esthetics than the max canine and may require extra {{c1::radiographic views}} if bifurcated.
The mandibular 1st premolar has 2 cusps: buccal {{c1::large}}, lingual {{c2::small/nonfunctional}}; it has 1 root.
The mandibular 1st premolar has a prominent {{c1::transverse ridge}} with 2 defined mesial and distal pits on either side.
The {{c1::mandibular 1st premolar}} functions more like a canine; its {{c2::buccal}} cusp is the only functional cusp in occlusion.
The mandibular 2nd premolar has {{c1::2 or 3}} cusps and a square or round occlusal shape.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Lower 2 Premolar → L2P → LAP → take laps in the park with trees → three → L2P has three cusps.

cloze.text: Mandibular 2nd premolar groove pattern: 3-cusp form = {{c1::Y}}-shaped groove; 2-cusp form = {{c2::U or H}}-shaped groove.
The {{c1::3}}-cusp form of the mandibular 2nd premolar is more common.
The mandibular 2nd premolar is a common {{c1::extraction}} site for ortho.
The mandibular 1st molar's two roots are {{c1::mesial and distal}}.
The {{c1::mandibular 1st molar}} is the widest tooth mesiodistally and has complex occlusal anatomy.
The mandibular 1st molar is the {{c1::first permanent tooth to erupt}}; its {{c2::buccal pit}} is prone to decay.
Early loss of the mandibular 1st molar affects {{c1::molar relationships}}.
The mandibular 2nd molar has a {{c1::cross}}-shaped occlusal groove pattern.
The mandibular 2nd molar is easier to instrument than the 1st molar; it is a common site for plaque retention at the {{c1::buccal groove}}.
Crowns of mandibular premolars and molars have a {{c1::lingual}} inclination.
The most pronounced root concavity is on the {{c1::mesial}} surface of the {{c2::maxillary 1st premolar}}; this area is commonly missed during instrumentation.
Premolars usually have 2 cusps, except the {{c1::mandibular 2nd premolar}}, which may have 2 or 3 cusps.
Upper molars (except 3rd molars) have {{c1::oblique ridges}}, formed by the union of the distal cusp ridge of the {{c2::mesiolingual}} cusp and the triangular ridge of the {{c3::distobuccal}} cusp.
The CEJ is more prominent on {{c1::mesial}} surfaces than on distal surfaces.
Maxillary molars are wider {{c1::buccolingually}} than mesiodistally.
Mandibular molars are wider {{c1::mesiodistally}} than buccolingually.
Premolars are wider {{c1::buccolingually}} than mesiodistally.
{{c1::Canines}} are the longest teeth in the dentition when combining root and crown length.
Maxillary lateral incisors are prone to {{c1::lingual caries}} due to their deep lingual fossae and lingual pit.
Maxillary molars have three furcations ({{c1::buccal, mesial, distal}}); the {{c2::mesial}} furcation is the most difficult to access clinically.
Mandibular molars have two furcations ({{c1::buccal and lingual}}), both {{c2::more}} accessible than maxillary furcations.
The cingulum is {{c1::centered}} on maxillary central incisors and slightly {{c2::distal}} on mandibular lateral incisors.
Root inclination follows arch form: mandibular crowns tilt {{c1::lingually}}, maxillary molars tilt {{c2::buccally}}.
Maxillary 1st molars may have a {{c1::palatal groove}}, which can collect plaque and mimic a crack.
Canines provide {{c1::canine guidance}} and support the facial contour and {{c2::vertical dimension}}.
{{c1::Amelogenesis imperfecta}} affects the {{c2::enamel}}; dentinogenesis imperfecta and dentin dysplasia affect the {{c3::dentin}}.
Amelogenesis imperfecta appearance: teeth are {{c1::yellow, brown, or white}}; may be pitted, rough, thin, or missing enamel.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta appearance: teeth are {{c1::blue-gray, yellow-brown, translucent}}.
Dentin dysplasia appearance: teeth are {{c1::normal or discolored}}.
Amelogenesis imperfecta radiographic findings: {{c1::thin or no enamel}}; may show {{c2::taurodontism}}.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta radiographic findings: {{c1::bulbous}} crowns, {{c2::short}} roots, no pulp or {{c3::shell teeth}}.
Dentin dysplasia radiographic findings: {{c1::short or absent roots}}, weird pulp shapes ({{c2::crescent, thistle}}), and {{c3::pulp stones}}.
Tooth sensitivity: amelogenesis imperfecta — yes, due to {{c1::exposed dentin}}; dentinogenesis imperfecta — yes, when {{c2::enamel chips}}.
Enamel in dentinogenesis imperfecta is {{c1::abnormal}} — thin, soft, or absent.
Enamel in dentin dysplasia is {{c1::normal}} but fractures easily due to weak dentin.
Dentin: amelogenesis imperfecta — {{c1::normal}}; dentinogenesis imperfecta — abnormal, {{c2::soft and weak}}; dentin dysplasia — abnormal, {{c3::tubules absent}}.
Amelogenesis imperfecta Type I — {{c1::hypoplastic}}: enamel is too {{c2::thin}} but hard; may appear pitted or smooth.
Amelogenesis imperfecta Type II — {{c1::hypomaturation}}: enamel is normal in thickness but {{c2::soft and mottled}}; chips easily; explorer tip may penetrate.
Amelogenesis imperfecta Type III — {{c1::hypocalcified}}: enamel normal in thickness but very soft and yellow due to poor mineralization; {{c2::severe sensitivity}} and rapid wear.
Amelogenesis imperfecta Type IV: combination of {{c1::hypoplastic and hypomaturation}} features, often with {{c2::taurodontism}} (elongated pulp chambers).
Dentinogenesis imperfecta Type I occurs with {{c1::osteogenesis imperfecta}}; enamel fractures over soft dentin; no visible pulp.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta Type II: similar to Type I but with {{c1::no bone disease}}; radiographically identical.
Dentinogenesis imperfecta Type III ({{c1::Brandywine}}): very {{c2::large}} pulp chambers and extremely thin dentin walls — "{{c3::shell teeth}}."
Dentin dysplasia Type I ({{c1::radicular}}): crowns are normal; roots are {{c2::short/absent}}; early tooth loss, tooth mobility.
Dentin dysplasia Type II ({{c1::coronal}}): affects both pulp and crown; teeth discolored; pulp shows {{c2::thistle- or flame}}-shaped chambers and pulp stones.
Treatment of amelogenesis imperfecta, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and dentin dysplasia: restorative/aesthetic work, desensitizing agents, orthodontics; {{c1::bleaching}} is ineffective.
In hypodontia, the {{c1::permanent}} dentition is most commonly affected.
Most commonly missing teeth (hypodontia): {{c1::permanent third molars}}, then {{c2::maxillary lateral incisors}}, then {{c3::mandibular second premolars}}.
The second most common supernumerary tooth is the {{c1::maxillary fourth molar (distomolar)}}.
{{c1::Localized}} microdontia (a single tooth, e.g. peg lateral) is more common than generalized microdontia.
Localized macrodontia affecting one side of the dental arch is called {{c1::facial hemihypertrophy}}.
In gemination, the crown is divided by a {{c1::notched}} area and can appear wide; there is {{c2::one}} root and one common pulp.
In fusion, the two crowns appear as a single large crown; roots may be {{c1::separated or fused}}.
Gemination and fusion both carry a risk for {{c1::infection and caries}}.
Concrescence most often involves adjacent {{c1::maxillary molars}}.
Enamel pearls are usually found on {{c1::molars}} near the root {{c2::bifurcation or trifurcation}}.
An enamel pearl may be mistaken for {{c1::calculus}}, pulp stone, or restorations, and can be problematic with {{c2::periodontal}} treatment.
Hypercementosis may be associated with trauma, occlusal forces, inflammation, {{c1::Paget's disease}}, arthritis, and {{c2::aging}}.
Hypercementosis needs no treatment, but {{c1::extraction}} may be more difficult due to thickened roots.
Dilaceration may complicate extraction or {{c1::endodontic}} therapy.
Taurodontism usually affects a single molar or several {{c1::molars in the same quadrant}}.
Taurodontism is associated with amelogenesis imperfecta (especially {{c1::hypomaturation}} type) and {{c2::Down syndrome}}.
Radiographically, dens in dente shows a {{c1::radiopaque or tooth-like structure}} within the crown.
Dens in dente is most commonly seen in {{c1::maxillary lateral incisors}}; the tooth is more vulnerable to caries and infections, including {{c2::periapical lesions}}.
Talon cusp issues include malocclusion, {{c1::pulpal infection}} due to fracture or wear of the cusp, speech problems, and injuries to the lips and tongue.
Ankylosis most often affects {{c1::deciduous molars}}.
An ankylosed tooth appears {{c1::submerged}} and has a {{c2::solid}} sound when percussed.
Erosion key features: {{c1::smooth, cupped, shiny}} lesions; enamel loss; flat occlusal surface; on {{c2::facial/lingual}} surfaces of multiple teeth.
Abrasion key features: {{c1::notched, hard}} lesions at the cervical margin; commonly on {{c2::buccal cervical margins}}, especially on roots.
Abfraction key features: sharp {{c1::V-shaped or wedge-shaped}} lesions at the {{c2::cervical third}} (buccal).
cloze.extra: Board Alert: abfraction and abrasion are extremely hard to tell apart from clinical images alone — use keywords like "habits" (abrasion) or "V-shape" (abfraction).

cloze.text: Attrition key features: {{c1::flattened}} surfaces; wear matches {{c2::opposing teeth}}; on incisal edges and occlusal cusps.
Erosion clinical note: ask if the patient drinks water with {{c1::lemon}} (can erode facial surfaces); also seen in drug use such as {{c2::methamphetamine}}.
Occlusal stress causes abfractions and can also cause subsequent {{c1::dislodging of restorations}} placed on the abfraction site.
The first sign of attrition is the disappearance of {{c1::mamelons}} on anterior teeth and {{c2::flattening of occlusal cusps}} on molars.
In internal resorption, {{c1::dentin or cementum}} becomes absorbed into the tooth canal, causing the tooth's inner and outer surfaces to become inflamed.
A {{c1::pink/red}} appearance of a tooth is a sign of {{c2::internal resorption}}.
Prevalence of dentin dysplasia: about 1 in {{c1::100,000}}.
Prevalence of dentinogenesis imperfecta: about 1 in {{c1::6,000–8,000}}.
Prevalence of amelogenesis imperfecta: about 1 in {{c1::700–14,000}}.
cloze.extra: Rank: DI (commonest of the dentin disorders) is far more common than DD (rarest).

basic.front: Why does dentin dysplasia cause no tooth sensitivity?
basic.back: Dentinal tubules / odontoblastic processes are absent.

basic.front: How do you tell fusion from gemination clinically?
basic.back: Count the teeth: in fusion one tooth is "missing" from the count; in gemination the count is normal.

basic.front: Why must an ankylosed primary molar usually be extracted?
basic.back: It will not exfoliate, so it blocks eruption of the permanent successor (unless that tooth is congenitally missing).

basic.front: Board question: how do you tell abrasion from abfraction?
basic.back: Look for keywords — "habits" (toothbrush, toothpick, objects) → abrasion; "V-shape"/wedge, occlusal stress → abfraction. Clinical images alone barely differ.
basic.extra: Board Alert. Clinical note: ask patients about their habits.

One or more teeth larger than normal
A single tooth germ attempts to divide → incomplete formation of two teeth (notched wide crown, one root, one pulp)
Two tooth buds join during development to form a single, larger tooth
Two adjacent teeth united by cementum only (at the roots)
A small, spherical enamel projection on a root surface
Excessive cementum deposition on the roots, typically at the apex

Teeth with elongated, large pulp chambers and short roots
The enamel organ invaginates into the crown of a tooth before mineralization
An accessory enamel cusp on the occlusal surface (a pulp horn may extend into it)
Dens evaginatus on an anterior tooth (may contain pulp)
The tooth is fused to bone
Loss of tooth structure from acid exposure (intrinsic: vomiting, GERD; extrinsic: diet, environment)
Loss of tooth structure from mechanical friction (toothbrush, toothpick, foreign objects)
Occlusal stress causes flexure and microfracture at the cervical area
Wear from tooth-to-tooth contact (normal chewing or bruxism)
basic.extra: Did you know: attrition is normal wear; grinding is pathologic and can cause loss of tooth structure.

basic.back: Part of the tooth's external surface is lost (orthodontics, trauma)
Internal tooth structure is lost (pulpal injury, trauma, heat, chemicals)

mcq.question: During a periodontal exam of a maxillary first molar with furcation involvement, which furcation is MOST difficult to access with instruments?
mcq.explanation: Maxillary molars have three furcations (buccal, mesial, distal); the mesial (approached from the palatal) is the hardest to reach. The buccal is the most accessible; a "lingual" furcation belongs to mandibular molars.

mcq.question: A 7-year-old's recently erupted lower posterior tooth has five cusps and early decalcification in a buccal pit. Which tooth is this most likely?
mcq.explanation: The mandibular 1st molar is the first permanent tooth to erupt, has 5 cusps (MB, DB, D, ML, DL), and its buccal pit is caries-prone. The mandibular 2nd molar has only 4 cusps and erupts years later.

mcq.question: All of the following statements about crown proportions are true EXCEPT one. Which is the EXCEPTION?
options: A. Maxillary molars are wider buccolingually than mesiodistally
B. Mandibular molars are wider mesiodistally than buccolingually
C. Premolars are wider mesiodistally than buccolingually
D. The CEJ curvature is more prominent on mesial than distal surfaces
mcq.answer: C. Premolars are wider mesiodistally than buccolingually
mcq.explanation: Premolars are wider BUCCOLINGUALLY than mesiodistally (like maxillary molars). Only mandibular molars are wider mesiodistally.

mcq.question: A 10-year-old with a history of multiple bone fractures has opalescent blue-gray teeth. Radiographs show bulbous crowns, short roots and obliterated pulp chambers. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Blue-gray translucent teeth with bulbous crowns and no visible pulp = dentinogenesis imperfecta; with bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta) it is Type I. Type III shows LARGE pulp chambers ("shell teeth"), not obliterated ones.

mcq.question: A 14-year-old has normal-looking crowns but several mobile teeth. Radiographs show very short roots and crescent-shaped pulp remnants. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Dentin dysplasia Type I (radicular): crowns normal, roots short/absent, early mobility and tooth loss. Type II (coronal) gives discoloured crowns with thistle/flame-shaped pulps and pulp stones.

mcq.question: A radiograph of a 7-year-old with a diastema shows an unerupted, small conical tooth between the maxillary central incisors. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: A mesiodens is the most common supernumerary tooth and lies between the maxillary central incisors; supernumeraries are typically small and often fail to erupt. A distomolar (2nd most common) lies distal to the 3rd molar.

mcq.question: A maxillary central incisor has an unusually wide crown with an incisal notch. The radiograph shows one root and one pulp canal, and the tooth count is normal. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Gemination: one tooth germ tries to divide — notched wide crown, one root, one pulp, normal count. In fusion two buds join, so the count is one tooth short.

mcq.question: While exploring the furcation of a mandibular molar, the hygienist feels a smooth, hard, round nodule that cannot be removed by scaling. The radiograph shows a small, round radiopacity at the furcation. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: An enamel pearl is a spherical enamel projection on the root near a bi/trifurcation of molars; it can be mistaken for calculus but will not scale off. Hypercementosis thickens the root, usually at the apex.

mcq.question: Radiographs of a patient with Down syndrome show mandibular molars with very tall pulp chambers and short roots. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Taurodontism = elongated, large pulp chambers with short roots, associated with Down syndrome and amelogenesis imperfecta. Dentin dysplasia shows obliterated or thistle-shaped pulps, not enlarged ones.

mcq.question: A periapical radiograph of a maxillary lateral incisor shows a radiopaque, tooth-like structure inside the crown and a periapical radiolucency. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Dens in dente (dens invaginatus) shows a "tooth within a tooth", most often in maxillary lateral incisors, and predisposes to caries and periapical lesions. A talon cusp is an extra cusp projecting from an anterior tooth, not inside the crown.

mcq.question: An 11-year-old's mandibular primary second molar sits well below the occlusal plane of the adjacent teeth and gives a solid sound on percussion. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: An ankylosed tooth is fused to bone, appears submerged and sounds solid on percussion; deciduous molars are most often affected. Concrescence joins two teeth by cementum, not tooth to bone.

mcq.question: A patient who sips lemon water throughout the day has smooth, shiny loss of enamel on the facial surfaces of many teeth. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Erosion is chemical (acid) loss — smooth, cupped, shiny lesions on facial/lingual surfaces of multiple teeth; lemon water erodes facial surfaces. Abrasion is mechanical and gives notched cervical lesions.

mcq.question: A patient with heavy occlusal contacts and no unusual oral habits has sharp, wedge-shaped lesions at the buccal cervical third of several premolars; a previous restoration at one site has dislodged. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Abfraction: occlusal stress causes cervical flexure → V/wedge-shaped lesions, and restorations placed there tend to dislodge. Abrasion would come with a habit history (toothbrush, toothpick) — the Board Alert keyword.

mcq.question: A patient reports a pink discoloration of the crown of a maxillary central incisor that was traumatized two years ago. Which is most likely?
mcq.explanation: A pink/red tooth is the sign of internal resorption (pulpal injury or trauma — the resorbing pulp shows through the crown). External resorption affects the outer root surface, often after orthodontics.
